title: A Front Divided
subtitle: The unfinished campaign and the human consequences of occupation
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: On 25 August, the turn south coexisted with renewed Soviet attacks and battles from Lake Ilmen to Odessa. The closing study weighs continued resistance, coercion, the murder of Jewish children at Bila Tserkva and the coalition’s expanding external connections.
body:
At 02:35 on 25 August 1941, Stalin and Shaposhnikov ordered the Western Front to continue attacking the German grouping around Smolensk. The directive assigned objectives to six armies and required cooperation with the Reserve Front. That same day, German forces were beginning the larger southward operation authorised on 21 August. The two offensives belonged to the same strategic situation. Germany could redirect its principal mobile effort without making the centre quiet; the Soviet command could order renewed pressure there without removing the danger to Ukraine. [1] [2]a

On 25 August, Soviet forces were withdrawing and regrouping south of Lake Ilmen, Tallinn depended chiefly on its sea connection, and Odessa continued to resist. German victories had opened territory to occupation without ending the war. Commands still awaited replacements and supplies. Tallinn’s evacuation, the first Arctic convoy’s arrival and the September battles lay ahead.

Smolensk remained a battlefield

Stavka interpreted the German concentration against Bryansk Front as apparently directed towards Bryansk and Zhizdra, while other German forces held the Bely, Vyazma and Spas-Demensk directions. Its assessment recognized a danger without resolving the intended German movement. Commanders had to answer several plausible threats while trying to exploit the commitment of German forces elsewhere.[1]

The Western Front’s response was to keep pressure on the German position around Smolensk. The 29th Army was directed toward Velizh. The 30th was to support the 19th Army’s attack on Dukhovshchina, north of Smolensk. The 19th Army was then to turn southwest toward the city’s area while avoiding a frontal assault on Smolensk itself. This sequence sought to undo the German position through connected movements, rather than simply send all available troops toward the same urban objective. The northern approach, the city’s communications and the neighbouring armies’ progress had to be understood together. [1]

South and east of those formations, the 16th Army was to attack toward Kardymovo and Smolensk in support of the 19th and 20th Armies. The 20th Army’s initial direction ran through the Klimova and Ryabtsevo station areas before turning northwest. These orders attempted to create converging pressure against the Smolensk–Yartsevo grouping. A railway station in such a directive was more than a convenient place name: it marked a communications point around which movement, supply and defensive positions might be organised. Reaching it required fighting through the German forces protecting the same network. [1]b

The 22nd Army had a different and urgent responsibility. It was ordered to deal with German mobile forces that had penetrated its area and to secure the offensive’s northern flank around the Velikiye Luki sector. Air and tank support were specified for this task. The wider attack therefore depended partly on restoring a situation already deteriorating at one end of the front. A headquarters could order offensive action in the centre while requiring defensive recovery on its flank, but both tasks competed for the limited formations and supporting arms available. [1]

The execution provisions sought to prevent the disconnections that had impaired earlier attacks. Continuous reconnaissance of open flanks would improve warning; immediate fortification of captured positions would help retain gains; coordinated infantry, artillery, tank and air action would connect fire support to movement. These were interdependent requirements. A formation that advanced without securing its new position might lose the ground before the next stage began, while support arriving at the wrong time could leave infantry exposed. The directive records an effort to apply experience, with actual improvement depending on whether formations possessed the staff work, training and equipment needed to realise it. [1]c

What the centre could still sustain

The planned offensive also required cooperation with Zhukov’s Reserve Front. Its left wing was to attack from 30 August, with the 24th Army directed against the Yelnya grouping and toward Pochinok, and the 43rd Army toward Roslavl. Those were future tasks as seen on 25 August. The broader Smolensk campaign therefore extended beyond this study’s endpoint, and the later fighting around Yelnya cannot be treated as already completed. The directive simultaneously required the Reserve Front to continue developing a deeper defensive belt. Preparation for attack and preparation for another German advance existed within the same order. [1]

The German centre consequently retained important obligations while its principal mobile effort shifted south. Infantry had to hold the existing line, artillery had to support that defence, and reserves had to respond to Soviet penetrations. The forces protecting the southern movement’s flank were also unavailable for other tasks. The image of a complete pause before Moscow obscures this expenditure. Even where an army group gained little territory, fighting could continue to consume ammunition, experienced infantry, vehicles and the time needed to rebuild units for a later offensive. [2]d

German personnel accounting provides a useful distinction between replacements assigned and replacements received. The Army’s retrospective study records 146,000 replacements reaching the eastern theatre between 22 June and 25 August: 66,000 for Army Group Centre, 52,000 for South and 28,000 for North. The same table separately lists further arrivals during 25–31 August and men still expected afterward. Those later categories cannot be added to the strength available on the twenty-fifth. The table illustrates a recurring problem throughout this phase: resources existed at several points in a system, but only some had reached the formations that needed them. [3]

The table’s distinction between arrivals and expectations keeps the replacement figures within their proper limits. A man who had reached the eastern theatre had not necessarily reached the company that needed him; a formation could receive replacements while losing other men in continuing combat. The figures therefore cannot be subtracted from a casualty total assembled on another date to produce a precise measure of fighting strength. They document an effort to replenish the army. Its usefulness depended on where those men went and what the receiving formations still possessed in weapons, officers and supporting services. [3]e

Soviet recovery was visible in the continuing ability to assign armies another offensive, but that capacity also needs definition. The directive specified coordination, reconnaissance and support because these had been practical weaknesses in earlier attacks. It did not prove that they had been overcome. The German centre faced a real military obligation to hold against renewed pressure; the Soviet command faced the equally real problem of making that pressure converge. By late August, the persistence of both problems mattered more than either side’s expectation that the next order would finally resolve them. [2] [1]f

Retreat and recovery south of Lake Ilmen

The northern front supplied a particularly clear record of what such adaptation looked like under pressure. The counteroffensive around Staraya Russa had forced a German response, but by 23–25 August the Soviet 11th Army was withdrawing behind the Lovat. Its war diary describes a relatively organised movement by its own formations alongside serious disorder in the neighbouring 34th Army. These descriptions come from one army’s headquarters and need to retain that perspective. They nevertheless show why the outcome cannot be reduced to a single arrow moving eastward across the map. [4]

The 180th and 254th Rifle Divisions were assigned sectors on the eastern bank of the Lovat, while the 182nd and 183rd Divisions were to assemble farther back in army reserve. Elements remained temporarily at crossings and bridgeheads until relieving units arrived. The 21st Motorised Rifle Regiment also crossed to the eastern bank and covered a broad sector by blocking the most important approaches. This was a defence organised around usable routes rather than a uniformly occupied line. The river provided an obstacle, but the army still had to control crossing places and maintain contact between its reduced formations. [4]

Movement was restricted by air attack and the need to conceal troops. The diary records an instruction preventing units from continuing their marches in daylight on 24 August; they were to remain where dawn found them and resume after darkness. This restriction changed the pace of withdrawal and regrouping. A division ordered to assemble farther east could be physically moving toward its destination while remaining unavailable there for much of the day. The resulting delay was not explained by distance alone. Air superiority affected the hours during which roads could be used and therefore the rate at which a new defence could be established. [4]

A liaison report received by 25 August described soldiers of the 34th Army scattered along roads and in woods. The 11th Army lacked reliable information about its neighbour and recorded efforts to collect men and rebuild formations. The journal documents serious disintegration. It does not establish how many had deliberately deserted and how many had become separated under attack.[4]g

Morozov’s missing division

Morozov’s 11th Army could not give the 202nd Motorised Division a definite task while headquarters did not know where it was. By the end of 24 August the diary placed it near Malye Dubovitsy. Morozov then sent a personal note ordering concentration near Bolshiye Dubovitsy by the following morning. Finding the division made coordination possible again, although the record does not prove that every element arrived on time.[4]h

The approaches to Leningrad and Tallinn

Farther north, Army Group North’s movement toward Leningrad remained divided among routes approaching from the west, the Luga area and the Lake Ilmen sector. Soviet resistance and the counterattacks farther south complicated the concentration of German forces. The difficulty was not simply taking the next town. An advancing force had to keep its connections open while neighbouring formations dealt with different terrain and different enemy groupings. The fighting near Staraya Russa mattered to Leningrad because it competed for German strength that might otherwise have supported the advance toward the city. [3]i

Tallinn presented a separate coastal problem. German forces had reached the Gulf of Finland near Kunda on 7 August, cutting the land connection from Tallinn toward Leningrad. The remaining Soviet position depended on maritime communications. Within that position were military formations, naval personnel, industrial workers and civilians with sharply different relationships to Soviet power. The Estonian Maritime Museum’s account emphasises that thousands of Estonian men had been compulsorily mobilised. A ship leaving the port could therefore carry people escaping German attack alongside people being removed from their country against their will. [5]

The approach to Tallinn also required infantry fighting that an image of uninterrupted German mechanised advance would miss. Toomas Hiio’s study of the Kiviloo battle identifies the 3rd Battalion of the German 162nd Infantry Regiment, 61st Infantry Division, fighting on 22 August against elements of the 1st Estonian Rifle Regiment formed from Soviet destruction battalions. Those forces were covering a withdrawal toward Tallinn. Hiio also shows how the sparse road and railway network constrained the movement of German infantry, ammunition and supplies, while air support competed with priorities toward Leningrad. Local action and transport capacity helped determine the pace of the larger advance. [6]

Tallinn’s major evacuation remained ahead on 25 August. The convoys departed on the twenty-eighth, and the maritime disaster near Juminda unfolded on 28–29 August. The prior loss of land communications had already made the port dependent on a sea exit, but the future losses cannot be treated as knowledge shared by those preparing to leave. Commanders had to preserve an embarkation area while organising shipping. For civilians and forcibly mobilised men, access to that shipping could combine escape from German attack with removal under Soviet authority. The meaning of departure depended on the person’s circumstances as well as on the operation’s military purpose. [5]j

The work of preparing a city

Lena Mukhina before the blockade

Lena Mukhina’s diary records three hours unloading a barge of bricks on 5 July as compulsory labour, and four hours digging trenches by the Obvodny Canal on 9 August. Her entries also preserve concern for her mother. These dated extracts, published in Russian by Ogonyok, connect the city’s defensive preparations with one young resident’s work. They do not measure all her labour or every resident’s experience.[7]k

Ukraine after Uman

In the south, the destruction of the Soviet grouping around Uman had removed a major obstacle to the German advance, but it had not completed Army Group South’s objectives. Soviet forces withdrawing eastward sought to preserve crossings over the Dnieper and establish another line. German plans called for bridgeheads at places including Cherkassy, Kremenchug and Dnepropetrovsk. Each crossing offered access to further operations while creating a new position that had to be supplied and defended. A bridgehead was the beginning of another logistical problem as well as an operational opportunity. [3]

Kiev remained connected to a different danger. The German 6th Army faced resistance around the city and from the Soviet 5th Army farther north, while the advance of the 2nd Army and 2nd Panzer Group from the Gomel direction threatened the wider rear. The strategic choice examined in The Decision to Turn South was now becoming a movement that Soviet commands had to counter. The Soviet Central Front was being dissolved and its surviving forces incorporated into the Bryansk Front, adding another organisational transition to an already unstable operational situation. [2]

A headquarters change had immediate consequences for surviving units: which command would assign their next position, supply them and coordinate their neighbours? The reorganisation of the central and Bryansk sectors sought to answer those questions as the German threat shifted. It could not restore lost weapons or communications by itself. This is why the continuing existence of formations after Uman and Gomel matters without proving that a secure defence had been rebuilt. The Soviet state retained institutions through which another response could be attempted, while the troops entering them remained badly affected by the defeats. [2]l

Odessa remained a defended coastal position outside the main Soviet line. The Romanian 4th Army’s approach had developed into a sustained struggle, while the Soviet garrison retained a connection to the Black Sea Fleet. Stavka’s directive of 19 August placed Rear Admiral Gavriil Zhukov in command of the Odessa Defence Region under the fleet commander. The arrangement recognised the dependence of land defence on ships, coastal facilities and maritime supply. It offered an organisational answer to the problem of coordinating services whose immediate responsibilities had previously been divided. [8] [9]m

Civilians within the operational system

Leningrad’s preparations and Tallinn’s departure drew civilians into military work through different forms of authority. Mukhina recorded compulsory labour alongside a desire to help. For Estonian men, Soviet mobilization could mean removal from their country against their will. The armies’ needs for transport and labour reached far beyond their fighting formations, without making these experiences identical.

At Belaya Tserkov (now Bila Tserkva), south of Kiev, German army officers confronted the imminent murder of Jewish children. After members of Einsatzgruppe C murdered Jewish adults in August, approximately ninety children were held in a building. The German Silent Heroes Memorial Centre dates their murder to 22 August and records that the commander of the 6th Army, Walther von Reichenau, approved continuation of the killing after a temporary postponement. These children were murdered before the great September encirclement of Kiev. Their fate belongs to this phase of the advance, not only to the later history of occupation.[15]

Helmuth Groscurth’s report of 21 August makes the army’s involvement harder to simplify. Alerted by divisional chaplains, he visited the children on 20 August and questioned the authority for killing them. His account also sought to prevent nearby soldiers from witnessing the proceedings, offered divisional troops if additional guards were needed, and accepted in its concluding reasoning that the children’s deaths followed from the killing of their parents. This is an intervention within a criminal operation, not an unambiguous refusal of genocide. It establishes knowledge and choices within army offices, alongside the security-police killing apparatus and Ukrainian guards described in the report. Neither the presence of protest nor the division of institutional roles absolves the decision to allow the murder to proceed.[16]

The memorial account stresses Groscurth’s attempt to save the children; his own report preserves more compromised reasoning, including concern for German troops. Both are evidence of his intervention. The postponement did not become rescue, and Reichenau’s approval allowed the killings to proceed. Nothing in these records establishes a divisional mutiny or a common motive among everyone who knew of the children.[15][16]n

Order No. 270 threatened families through its classifications of capture and desertion. The northern army diary, by contrast, records scattered men without determining why each was missing. Such punitive categories could conceal the disorder commanders were trying to overcome. This Soviet policy and German persecution require their own evidence and distinct accounts of responsibility.[10]o

The war’s external connections

The effort to sustain the Soviet Union was beginning to take a more tangible maritime form. Convoy Dervish had departed Liverpool on 12 August and continued from Iceland on the twenty-first, bound for Archangel. On 25 August it was still in transit; it would arrive on 31 August. That sequence prevents the convoy’s cargo from being counted as supplies already available to the armies described here. It also shows how the campaign was becoming connected to a longer transport system involving merchant shipping, naval escorts, ports and onward distribution. Political agreement was only the beginning of that chain. [11]p

On the study’s anchor date, Britain and the Soviet Union also invaded Iran. Reza Shah appealed to Roosevelt on 25 August, presenting the attack as aggression against a neutral country and rejecting the invading governments’ justification concerning Germans resident in Iran. His appeal invoked international justice and the rights of peoples. The document records Iran’s ruler making a diplomatic case for intervention; it is not an independent account of every military incident he described. It nevertheless places Iranian sovereignty and civilian exposure to attack within a story often told only as the development of Allied cooperation. [12]

The American minister in Tehran, Louis Dreyfus, reported that the Shah had offered further assurances about expelling Germans and asked what Britain and the Soviet Union would provide in return for his concessions. Dreyfus also stated that reliable news of the fighting was still lacking, while describing comparatively normal activity in Tehran and British aircraft dropping leaflets. The report preserves the uneven information available during the opening day. Diplomatic discussions, military intervention and daily urban life were proceeding simultaneously, and observers in the capital could not yet offer a complete account of the invasion’s effects. [13]

Concern extended beyond Iran. In Washington, the Turkish ambassador Mehmet Münir Ertegün told Wallace Murray that he feared the consequences of expanding Soviet power and doubted British assurances. He expressly spoke without instructions from his government, so his remarks cannot be presented as an official Turkish policy decision. They show the anxiety that cooperation against Germany could generate in neighbouring states. The alliance’s strategic purposes did not dissolve other countries’ concerns about sovereignty, territorial security or the possibility that their interests would be sacrificed to the larger war. [14]q

The position on 25 August

On 25 August Germany could still concentrate forces for another devastating offensive. It had not destroyed the Soviet Union’s capacity to wage war. Across this phase, Soviet headquarters had lost armies, rebuilt commands, attempted relief and renewed attacks; German headquarters had won major battles while confronting an opponent that continued to field forces. The cost of that persistence was borne by particular people: wounded men seeking a route to treatment, prisoners entering German custody, families leaving cities, and communities whose capture exposed them to murder.

The turn south threatened Kiev’s communications while renewed Soviet attacks tested German forces remaining around Smolensk. Leningrad’s approaches and Tallinn’s sea exit were still contested. The invasion had penetrated deep into Soviet territory and intensified occupation violence, yet the first great encirclements had failed to end organized Soviet resistance. The next phase follows the operations that would test those unresolved positions.

sourceMethod: Lettered evidence notes retain detailed references and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the sources below. Published Soviet transcriptions distinguish orders from reported results; archival locators do not imply direct inspection of original files. Contemporary claims, later testimony and historical interpretations are attributed separately. Where only an abstract, extract or reproduced text was available, that limit remains stated in the notes. The dated map has separate feature sources and precision notes.
